title: Hidden engines in tidal disruption events: multimessenger signatures in a lepto-hadronic framework

paper.title:
Hidden engines in tidal disruption events:
multimessenger signatures in a lepto-hadronic framework
paper.abstract: Abstract Tidal disruption events (TDEs) provide a unique laboratory for studying transient accretion, outflows, particle acceleration, and the possible connection between stellar disruptions and high-energy neutrinos. Motivated by recent candidate TDE–neutrino associations and by the forthcoming sensitivity of multimessenger facilities, we investigate under which physical conditions TDEs can be detected in MeV, GeV, and TeV gamma rays, and in high-energy neutrinos. We develop a lepto-hadronic emission framework and apply it to three representative sources: AT2019dsg, AT2019ehz, and ASASSN-14li. For each source we explore a set of physically motivated models that vary the proton and electron spectral indices, the minimum Lorentz factor of non-thermal protons, the particle energy partition, the acceleration efficiency, the magnetic compactness, and the presence of a compact corona. We compute the broadband spectral energy distributions, the associated muon-neutrino spectra, and compare them with reference sensitivities for COSI, Fermi/LAT, CTAO, and KM3NeT/ARCA. We find that hard proton spectra and/or large minimum proton Lorentz factors are the most favourable conditions for TeV gamma-ray and neutrino detectability, while GeV-bright models can be predominantly leptonic and neutrino quiet. AT2019dsg and AT2019ehz can reach the CTAO and KM3NeT benchmarks in hadronically favourable configurations, whereas ASASSN-14li is more naturally bright in the MeV–GeV band and constrained by its radio synchrotron emission. Our results highlight the importance of combining MeV, GeV, TeV, radio, and neutrino observations to distinguish between transparent, hidden, and lepton-dominated TDE emission regimes.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Tidal disruption events (TDEs) occur when a star is scattered close enough to a massive black hole that the tidal force exceeds the star’s self-gravity. A fraction of the stellar debris remains bound, returns to pericenter, circularizes, and can power a luminous flare from the otherwise faint nucleus of a galaxy ( Rees, 1988 ) . Because the debris initially falls back at highly super-Eddington rates for many systems, TDEs provide a transient view of accretion, outflows, shocks, and non-thermal particle acceleration around massive black holes. Wide-field optical surveys and rapid multiwavelength follow-up have shown that TDEs are not a single observational class: some events are dominated by optical/UV emission, some are X-ray bright, some launch radio-emitting outflows or jets, and only a few have been discussed as possible high-energy neutrino emitters ( Langis and others, 2026 ) . The origin of the optical/UV emission remains one of the central open questions in TDE physics. In the simplest picture, the observed luminosity would trace efficient accretion of the fallback material, but the radiated energy and characteristic temperatures of optical TDEs are often difficult to reconcile with a bare, compact, steady thin disc ( Mummery et al., 2025 ) . Several alternatives have therefore been proposed. The optical/UV flare may be powered, at least partly, by shocks produced during stream self-intersection and circularization ( Shiokawa et al., 2015 ; Piran et al., 2015 ) ; by reprocessing of inner-disc or coronal radiation in an extended photosphere, wind, or debris layer; or by a combination of accretion, shocks, and outflow emission whose relative importance changes with time and viewing angle. Magnetic fields can further modify this picture by affecting the returning debris stream and the subsequent circularization flow ( Guillochon and McCourt, 2017 ; Bonnerot et al., 2017 ) . Recent optical polarimetric observations have strengthened the case that at least some TDEs require non-axisymmetric geometries and shock-powered emission during disc formation ( Liodakis and others, 2023 ; Koljonen and others, 2024 ; Koljonen et al., 2025 ; Floris and others, 2025 ; Floris and others, 2026 ) . These uncertainties are important for high-energy modelling because they determine the photon fields, magnetic fields, and compactness that control both particle cooling and γ \gamma -ray absorption. TDEs have also been proposed as sources of cosmic rays and high-energy neutrinos. Early studies focused on relativistic TDE jets and considered whether protons accelerated in internal shocks or external outflows could produce neutrinos through p γ \gamma and pp interactions ( Farrar and Gruzinov, 2009 ; Wang et al., 2011 ; Farrar and Piran, 2014 ; Wang and Liu, 2016 ; Dai and Fang, 2017 ; Senno et al., 2017 ; Lunardini and Winter, 2017 ; Guépin et al., 2018 ; Biehl et al., 2018 ) . Subsequent work showed that the same basic idea can be realised in several physical environments, including choked or off-axis jets, coronae, radiatively inefficient accretion flows, disc winds, and debris-interaction regions ( Hayasaki and Yamazaki, 2019 ; Murase et al., 2020 ; Liu et al., 2020 ; Fang et al., 2020 ; Winter and Lunardini, 2021 ; Matsumoto et al., 2022 ; Winter and Lunardini, 2023 ; Zheng et al., 2023 ; Mukhopadhyay et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Yuan et al., 2024 ) . These models differ in geometry, target photon field, baryon loading, and internal opacity, but they share a common observational challenge: neutrino production is accompanied by electromagnetic cascades, and the escaping γ \gamma -ray emission must remain consistent with X-ray, MeV, GeV, and TeV constraints. The possible association of AT2019dsg with IceCube-191001A brought this question into sharper focus ( Stein and others, 2021 ) . Further candidate associations involving accretion flares or TDE-like nuclear transients, such as AT2019fdr and AT2019aalc, have strengthened the motivation for considering TDEs as neutrino sources ( Reusch and others, 2022 ; van Velzen and others, 2024 ) . At the same time, the statistical significance of individual associations remains debated. Updated IceCube event catalogues, Fermi /LAT non-detections, and population-level correlation studies all indicate that current TDE–neutrino associations should be treated as suggestive rather than established ( Peng et al., 2022 ; Abbasi and others, 2025 ; Lu et al., 2025 ; Langis et al., 2026 ; Mukhopadhyay et al., 2026 ) . This motivates a question that is broader than the interpretation of any single event: under which physical conditions should a TDE be detectable in γ \gamma rays and neutrinos at all? A particularly useful diagnostic is the energy band in which the non-thermal power escapes. If the source is transparent, pion-decay emission and inverse-Compton radiation can appear in the GeV–TeV range and may be constrained by Fermi /LAT or detected by CTAO. If the source is compact and photon rich, the same hadronic activity can be hidden at TeV energies and reprocessed into the hard X-ray or MeV band through pair production and electromagnetic cascades ( Murase et al., 2020 ; Yuan and Winter, 2023 ) . The MeV range is therefore a key bridge between thermal X-ray/UV emission and GeV–TeV searches. Future observations with the Compton Spectrometer and Imager (COSI) will be especially valuable for testing hidden or partially hidden TDE scenarios ( Tomsick and others, 2023 ) , while CTAO and KM3NeT/ARCA will probe complementary TeV γ \gamma -ray and TeV–PeV neutrino signatures ( Carosi et al., 2021 ; Aiello and others, 2024 ) . In this paper we explore the detectability of non-thermal emission from TDEs using a lepto-hadronic emission framework based on the steady-state multi-zone bhjet model and its hadronic extension ( Lucchini et al., 2022 ; Kantzas and others, 2020 ; Kantzas et al., 2023b ) . Our aim is not to obtain a unique fit to each source, nor to claim that any individual TDE must have produced a particular neutrino alert. Instead, each model is a representative or reference realization chosen to isolate a specific physical regime, such as MeV–GeV brightness, TeV transparency, neutrino production, or radio synchrotron consistency. We use these representative models to identify the combinations of particle acceleration, proton spectral shape, minimum proton Lorentz factor, energy partition, magnetic field, photon compactness, and coronal opacity that make a TDE visible to COSI, Fermi /LAT, CTAO, and KM3NeT. This parameter-space approach is designed to connect the intrinsic physics of the source to practical multimessenger detectability. The overplotted multiwavelength data are used to check whether the model normalization and spectral shape are broadly compatible with the observed emission during the selected epoch, but the models are not selected by minimizing a global likelihood or chi-square. We apply the model to three TDEs that represent different observational regimes. AT2019dsg is used as a neutrino-motivated benchmark because of its proposed association with IceCube-191001A and evidence for non-thermal activity. AT2019ehz is treated as a prompt optical/UV outburst case with X-ray follow-up, allowing us to test whether high-energy emission could accompany the main TDE flare even without an established neutrino association. Finally, ASASSN–14li provides an X-ray- and radio-bright benchmark. Its radio data constrain the low-energy synchrotron component and allow us to test whether primary electrons, secondary pairs, or proton synchrotron can contribute to the observed non-thermal emission. The paper is organized as follows. In Sect. 2 , we describe the lepto-hadronic model and the photon attenuation processes included in the calculations. In Sect. 3 , we summarize the multiwavelength data used for the three sources. In Sect. 4 , we present the model families, spectral energy distributions, neutrino predictions, and benchmark-proximity ratios for COSI, Fermi /LAT, CTAO, and KM3NeT. We discuss the physical interpretation and comparison with previous work in Sect. 5 , and we summarize our conclusions in Sect. 6 .

sections.heading: 2 Model
sections.text: We use a semi-analytical, steady-state lepto-hadronic model to calculate the intrinsic photon and neutrino emission from compact dissipation regions in TDE environments. The model follows the philosophy of bhjet , where the dynamical properties of the emitting plasma are coupled to radiative transfer, but it is adapted here to the geometry expected during the circularization and early accretion phase of a TDE rather than to a scale-invariant compact jet ( Lucchini et al., 2022 ) . The hadronic extension follows the treatment developed in Kantzas and others (2020) , where relativistic protons are accelerated together with electrons and interact with gas and radiation fields, producing secondary photons, pairs, and neutrinos. The goal of the present work is not to fit a unique solution for each source, but to identify the physical conditions under which the GeV-to-TeV γ \gamma -ray and neutrino emission can become observable.

sections.heading: 2.1 Geometry and dynamical assumptions
sections.text: We consider a TDE around a black hole of mass M BH M_{\rm BH} and define the gravitational radius as R g = G ​ M BH / c 2 R_{g}=GM_{\rm BH}/c^{2} . During the circularization of the stellar debris, shocks are expected to form in the accretion flow and/or in the stream-intersection region ( Shiokawa et al., 2015 ; Steinberg and Stone, 2024 ) . We describe the system with an accretion disk in the equatorial plane and use the angle θ \theta between the disk axis and the line of sight as the viewing angle. Thus, θ ≃ 0 ∘ \theta\simeq 0^{\circ} corresponds to a face-on system, whereas θ ≃ 90 ∘ \theta\simeq 90^{\circ} corresponds to an edge-on system. The disk is truncated at a characteristic radius R disk R_{\rm disk} and radiates with luminosity L disk L_{\rm disk} , with the thermal component peaking in the optical/UV band for the parameter range explored here. In addition to the disk radiation, we include a compact thermal corona. The corona is described by its radius R cor R_{\rm cor} , temperature T cor T_{\rm cor} , and Thomson optical depth τ cor \tau_{\rm cor} . The corresponding number density is n cor = τ cor / σ T ​ R cor n_{\rm cor}=\tau_{\rm cor}/\sigma_{T}R_{\rm cor} , where σ T \sigma_{T} is the Thomson cross section. Unless stated otherwise, we assume a charge-neutral plasma with equal numbers of thermal electrons and protons. The thermal electrons Comptonize the disk photons and provide an additional target field for inverse Compton scattering and photohadronic interactions. In the numerical examples below the coronal temperature should be interpreted as an electron thermal energy, k B ​ T cor k_{\rm B}T_{\rm cor} , and is therefore quoted in energy units. The dissipation region and the corona should not be interpreted as two independent acceleration zones. In the present implementation, non-thermal electrons and protons are accelerated only in the compact shock region located at radius R R . The corona, when included, acts as a thermal photon field and as a reservoir of thermal target protons for Compton scattering, photohadronic interactions, and pp interactions. Its characteristic radius is denoted by R cor R_{\rm cor} . Thus, models with R < R cor R<R_{\rm cor} correspond to dissipation embedded within the coronal environment, whereas models with R > R cor R>R_{\rm cor} place the shock outside the nominal coronal scale. This distinction affects the target photon density, the internal opacity, and the efficiency of hadronic interactions, but protons are not separately accelerated throughout the corona. We assume that a fraction of the power released during the TDE is dissipated in shocks located at a characteristic radius R R from the black hole. This radius also sets the escape length of particles from the acceleration region. The dissipated power available to non-thermal particles and magnetic fields is denoted by P TDE P_{\mathrm{TDE}} . We parametrize the partition between particle and magnetic pressure through the plasma beta, β = P particles / P magnetic \beta=P_{\rm particles}/P_{\rm magnetic} . Low values of β \beta correspond to magnetically dominated shocks, while high values of β \beta correspond to particle-dominated shocks. We further use the parameter η e \eta_{e} to control the relative amount of non-thermal power carried by electrons and protons. This parameter is important for the high-energy output because the GeV emission can be dominated by leptonic inverse Compton scattering, whereas the TeV and neutrino emission require an efficient hadronic component. The emitting region is treated as quasi-static in the source frame. Therefore, the calculations presented here do not include quantities associated with a relativistic jet. The framework is intended to describe compact disk/corona, circularization, or mildly outflowing shock regions rather than a fully relativistic jetted TDE.

sections.text: At the shocks, a fraction of the thermal particles is accelerated to non-thermal energies. We do not impose a specific microscopic acceleration mechanism, but instead parametrize the accelerated distributions as power laws with exponential cutoffs. For each particle species i = e , p i=e,p , we use d ​ N i d ​ E i = N 0 , i ​ E i − p i ​ exp ⁡ ( − E i E i , max ) , E i ≥ E i , min , \frac{{\rm d}N_{i}}{{\rm d}E_{i}}=N_{0,i}\,E_{i}^{-p_{i}}\exp\left(-\frac{E_{i}}{E_{i,{\rm max}}}\right),\qquad E_{i}\geq E_{i,{\rm min}}, (1) where p i p_{i} is a free parameter and N 0 , i N_{0,i} is fixed by the non-thermal power assigned to that species. Unless stated otherwise, the minimum electron energy is tied to the peak of the relativistic Maxwell-Jüttner distribution, while for protons we set γ p , min = 1 \gamma_{p,{\rm min}}=1 . Below E i , min E_{i,{\rm min}} , the electrons follow the thermal Maxwell-Jüttner distribution and the protons are assumed to remain cold. The maximum particle energy is calculated by comparing the acceleration time-scale with the relevant cooling and escape time-scales. We use the acceleration time-scale ( Jokipii, 1987 ) t acc ​ ( E i ) = 4 ​ E i 3 ​ f sc ​ e ​ c ​ B , t_{\rm acc}(E_{i})=\frac{4E_{i}}{3f_{\rm sc}ecB}, (2) where e e is the elementary charge, B B is the characteristic magnetic field strength in the acceleration region, and f sc ≲ 1 f_{\rm sc}\lesssim 1 is the acceleration efficiency parameter. The value of E i , max E_{i,{\rm max}} is obtained from t acc − 1 ​ ( E i , max ) = ∑ j t j − 1 ​ ( E i , max ) , t_{\rm acc}^{-1}(E_{i,{\rm max}})=\sum_{j}t_{j}^{-1}(E_{i,{\rm max}}), (3) where the sum includes synchrotron cooling, inverse Compton scattering, inelastic hadronic collisions, photohadronic losses, Bethe–Heitler losses, and escape, whenever these processes are relevant for the particle species under consideration. For the parameter space explored in this work, the maximum electron energy is typically set by synchrotron cooling, t acc − 1 ​ ( E e , max ) ≃ t syn − 1 ​ ( E e , max ) = σ T ​ B 2 ​ E e , max ​ β e 2 6 ​ π ​ m e 2 ​ c 3 , t_{\rm acc}^{-1}(E_{e,{\rm max}})\simeq t_{\rm syn}^{-1}(E_{e,{\rm max}})=\frac{\sigma_{T}B^{2}E_{e,{\rm max}}\beta_{e}^{2}}{6\pi m_{e}^{2}c^{3}}, (4) where β e ​ c \beta_{e}c is the electron velocity. By contrast, the maximum proton energy is often limited by escape from the acceleration region, t acc − 1 ​ ( E p , max ) ≃ t esc − 1 ​ ( E p , max ) = β p ​ c R , t_{\rm acc}^{-1}(E_{p,{\rm max}})\simeq t_{\rm esc}^{-1}(E_{p,{\rm max}})=\frac{\beta_{p}c}{R}, (5) although photohadronic and Bethe–Heitler losses can dominate in sufficiently compact and luminous radiation fields. The most important parameters controlling the highest photon and neutrino energies are therefore B B , R R , f sc f_{\rm sc} , L disk L_{\rm disk} , τ cor \tau_{\rm cor} , and T cor T_{\rm cor} . To calculate the normalization of the power-law of non-thermal particles, we assume that a fraction ε i \varepsilon_{i} of the injected power is injected to the non-thermal particles, with i = e i=e for electrons and i = p i=p for protons. Typically, the fraction ε i \varepsilon_{i} is 10% for other astrophysical sources ( Petropoulou et al., 2015 ; Murase et al., 2020 ; Kantzas and others, 2020 ; Kantzas et al., 2023a ) , hence, we adopt this value here as well unless we explicitly mention another value.

sections.heading: 2.5.5 Total effective optical depth
sections.text: The total local optical depth is the sum of the individual contributions, τ eff ​ ( E γ ) = τ γ ​ γ ​ ( E γ ) + τ KN ​ ( E γ ) + τ BH ​ ( E γ ) + τ pe ​ ( E γ ) . \tau_{\rm eff}(E_{\gamma})=\tau_{\gamma\gamma}(E_{\gamma})+\tau_{\rm KN}(E_{\gamma})+\tau_{\rm BH}(E_{\gamma})+\tau_{\rm pe}(E_{\gamma}). (21) The relative importance of these terms depends on photon energy, source geometry, viewing angle, coronal density, and the amount of cold gas along the line of sight. The same physical ingredients that enhance neutrino production, namely high gas density and high photon density, can therefore suppress the escaping γ \gamma -ray flux. This tension is central to the detectability problem addressed in this work: TDEs are most efficient neutrino sources when the hadronic interaction depth is high, but they are most promising TeV γ \gamma -ray sources when the pair-production and matter opacities are low enough for high-energy photons to escape. The optical depth in Eq. ( 21 ) describes attenuation local to the TDE environment. In the observed SEDs we also include attenuation by the extragalactic background light during propagation to Earth.

sections.heading: 3.1 Data preparation
sections.text: We test the newly developed model against three typical optical TDEs, AT2019dsg, AT2019ehz, ASASSN--14li, which have publicly available multi-wavelength observations spanning from radio to X-rays. For the infrared, optical, and UV observations, we utilised data from TDECat 1 1 1 https://github.com/dlangis/TDECat ( Langis and others, 2026 ) , while for the radio observations, we used data from the Open multiwavelength Transient Event Repository 2 2 2 https://otter.idies.jhu.edu/ ( Franz et al., 2026 , OTTER;) . In all cases, we utilised Swift BAT and UVOT ( Roming et al., 2005 ; Burrows et al., 2005 ) , Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer ( Wright et al., 2010 , WISE;) and Near-Earth Object WISE Reactivation ( Mainzer et al., 2011 ; Mainzer et al., 2014 , NEOWISE;) data, while for AT2019dsg and AT2019ehz we also included Zwicky Transient Facility ( Graham et al., 2019 ; Bellm et al., 2019 ; Masci et al., 2019 , ZTF;) g- and r-band light curves. For AT2019dsg, the Fermi/LAT upper limits reported by Peng et al. (2022) are above the predicted GeV fluxes of all models considered here; therefore, the explored configurations are not ruled out by the archival LAT non-detection. All data are shown in Fig. 10 for AT2019dsg and AT2019ehz, and Fig. 11 for ASASSN–14li. For all three TDEs, we correct the IR, optical and UV light curves for the host-galaxy contribution by converting from magnitude to flux, calculating the mean of the pre-flare light curve for the infrared and optical, and utilising one post-flare period for the UVOT light curves. This value is then subtracted from the full light curve. This process is shown for ASASSN–14li in Fig. 11 , where the UVOT and infrared pre-host-subtraction light curves are shown in the upper and lower panels respectively. The horizontal lines show the host contribution considered in each case. We note that after the host subtraction, we considered as detections the observations that had a signal-to-noise ratio larger than 3. sections.heading: 3.2 Different observational regimes
sections.text: The three TDEs considered here probe different observational regimes. For AT2019dsg, we focus on a delayed neutrino-motivated phase, MJD 58850 58850 – 59100 59100 . This source is the only object in our sample with a published high-energy neutrino association, namely IceCube-191001A, detected about 154 154 d after the optical/UV peak. Radio observations of AT2019dsg indicate non-thermal activity from a central engine, making it a natural benchmark for testing whether TDEs can produce detectable neutrino emission together with GeV-to-TeV gamma rays. For AT2019ehz, we instead model the prompt optical/UV outburst phase, MJD 58500 58500 – 58640 58640 . The source was classified as a TDE and was observed to be variable in Swift/XRT, but it does not have an established high-energy neutrino association. Sparse radio detections occur at much later epochs and therefore do not directly constrain the particle distribution during the interval modelled here. We therefore use AT2019ehz as a test case for whether γ \gamma rays and neutrino emission could accompany the main TDE outburst. sections.heading: 4 Multimessenger emission of AT2019dsg, AT2019ehz and ASASSN–14li
sections.text: In this section we apply the model described in Sec. 2 to three TDEs and examine the conditions under which they can become observable at high energies. The data shown in the SEDs are the quasi-simultaneous multi-wavelength points described in Sec. 3 . Since the plotted SEDs combine heterogeneous multiwavelength data, host-subtracted photometry, binned X-ray spectra, and non-simultaneous measurements within finite time windows, we do not use a global chi-square minimization to define the models. Such a statistic would be sensitive to band-dependent systematics, source variability, and the model-dependent construction of the unfolded X-ray SEDs. Nevertheless, to make the comparison with the data explicit, we report a reduced chi-square-like diagnostic, χ red 2 \chi^{2}_{\rm red} , for each model using the plotted data points and their reported uncertainties. We use this quantity only as an a posteriori consistency measure, not as a model-selection criterion. The high-energy sensitivity curves shown in the figures are used only as observational benchmarks. In particular, we use the predicted sensitivity of the Compton Spectrometer and Imager (COSI) from Tomsick and others (2023) . For neutrinos, the grey curves correspond to the nominal ten-year KM3NeT/ARCA230 point-source sensitivity ( Aiello and others, 2024 ) . Since a TDE is transient, these curves should not be interpreted as a direct discovery threshold; the relevant quantity for detectability is the expected number of events during the assumed active period. Our models calculate epoch-averaged emission states rather than time-dependent light curves. Microscopic particle timescales (acceleration, cooling, escape) are far shorter than the light-curve evolution windows (Figs. 10 and 11 ), hence, we treat the particle distributions as quasi-steady. Each model represents average active-region conditions rather than a point-by-point fit. Explicit time-dependent modeling (evolving L disk L_{\rm disk} , coronal compactness, shock parameters, and non-thermal injection) could modify estimated γ \gamma -ray and neutrino fluences by factors of a few to order-of-magnitude levels depending on variability and flare behavior. Consequently, while our framework checks if time-averaged fluences match event-level expectations, explaining time delays—such as IC191001A arriving ∼ 154 \sim 154 days post-peak in AT2019dsg —requires full time-dependent modeling of particle injection, photon field evolution, and opacity. The model families below are exploratory and source-tailored rather than a uniform parameter grid for all three TDEs. The three sources present different observational constraints and different motivating questions: AT2019dsg is treated as a neutrino-motivated delayed-phase case, AT2019ehz as a prompt-outburst high-energy detectability case, and ASASSN–14li as a radio/X-ray-bright system with strong constraints on the low-energy synchrotron component. We therefore choose the parameters in Tables 1 – 3 to probe the physical regimes most relevant to each source.

sections.heading: 4.5 Muon-neutrino predictions
5 Discussion
sections.text: In this work, we aim to map the regions of parameter space in which a TDE can become visible in COSI, Fermi /LAT, CTAO, and KM3NeT. This is important because the same non-thermal proton population produces both neutrinos and secondaries, but the escaping γ \gamma rays are strongly regulated by the local radiation field. In a transparent source, the neutral-pion component can reach the GeV-to-TeV band and may be observable by Fermi /LAT and/or CTAO. In a more compact or photon-rich source, the same intrinsic hadronic power can be reprocessed by γ ​ γ \gamma\gamma absorption, shifting part of the observable counterpart toward the X-ray or MeV–GeV range. Therefore, a non-detection in the TeV band does not necessarily imply a neutrino-quiet TDE; it may instead indicate that the source is opaque in TeV γ \gamma rays. A controlled comparison in which the same leptonic and hadronic parameter grid is applied to all three sources would be needed to fully disentangle intrinsic source properties from modelling choices. The present work instead identifies physically motivated detectability regimes for each source. Such a uniform-grid study, combined with time-dependent light-curve modelling, will be pursued in future work.

sections.heading: 5.1 Accelerated-proton parameter phase space
sections.text: Across the three sources, the most important particle parameters are those that define the shape of the non-thermal proton distribution. Hard proton spectra place a larger fraction of the injected proton power close to the photomeson threshold and therefore naturally enhance the multi-TeV neutrino and high-energy γ \gamma -ray components. This is why the reference hard-proton models of AT2019dsg and AT2019ehz can approach the KM3NeT/ARCA reference sensitivity without requiring the most extreme values of the non-thermal proton fraction. Softer proton spectra can still be viable, but only if the proton power is shifted toward higher energies by increasing γ p , min \gamma_{p,\rm min} , by increasing the fraction of dissipated power injected into non-thermal protons, or by increasing the acceleration efficiency so that protons reach the p ​ γ p\gamma regime before escaping, such as AT2019dsg Models B, C, and AT2019ehz Model C. The second controlling quantity is the compactness and spectrum of the target photon field. A disc or corona provides the soft photons needed for p ​ γ p\gamma interactions and can therefore raise the neutrino luminosity. At the same time, the same photon field increases the internal opacity of the source. This produces a natural tension: efficient neutrino production favours dense photon targets, whereas CTAO detectability requires that at least part of the GeV-to-TeV cascade can escape. The AT2019ehz models show this most clearly. For Model A, we use a cold coronal photon field that is efficient in both p ​ γ p\gamma interactions and internal reprocessing, while Model B, for which we remove the corona, becomes more transparent to GeV-to-TeV photons. The comparison suggests that CTAO detections should favour sources or phases in which the high-energy emission region is not deeply embedded in the densest part of the optical/UV/X-ray radiation field, such as AT2019ehz. The third controlling quantity is the magnetic field, which we probe indirectly through the plasma beta in the ASASSN–14li models. For the cases of AT2019dsg and AT2019ehz, we assume a plasma in energy equipartition, namely β = 1 \beta=1 . A lower plasma beta strengthens the magnetic field and can enhance synchrotron emission from protons and secondary pairs. This changes the electromagnetic counterpart without necessarily producing a brighter TeV signal. In ASASSN–14li Model C, for example, proton synchrotron and secondary-pair emission can contribute in the radio-to-infrared and GeV bands, while the source remains quiet for CTAO. This demonstrates that a magnetically enhanced hadronic model may be more visible through radio, MeV, or GeV diagnostics than through TeV γ \gamma rays.

sections.heading: 5.2 Comparison between the sources
sections.text: The three sources occupy different regions of the same parameter space. AT2019dsg is the most direct benchmark for a possible neutrino-associated optical TDE, but our results support a cautious interpretation. Several combinations of parameters can place the predicted ν μ + ν ¯ μ \nu_{\mu}+\bar{\nu}_{\mu} spectrum near the KM3NeT/ARCA reference curve. However, these combinations are not unique: a hard proton distribution, a large γ p , min \gamma_{p,\rm min} , a large non-thermal proton fraction, or efficient acceleration can all lead to similar neutrino levels. This degeneracy means that the neutrino prediction cannot be inferred from the bolometric TDE luminosity alone. It depends on how efficiently the TDE channels power into protons above the pion-production threshold and on how transparent the source is to the associated cascade emission. Within the source-tailored parameter space explored here, AT2019ehz provides the clearest example of a potentially TeV-bright TDE. The reference Model A combines a hard proton spectrum with a cold coronal photon field, producing a strong p ​ γ p\gamma component and a multi-TeV neutrino spectrum. The no-corona hard-proton Model B is even more transparent and is therefore the most favorable case for simultaneous Fermi /LAT, CTAO, and KM3NeT searches. The soft-proton models remain viable only after the low-energy part of the proton distribution is suppressed or the non-thermal proton fraction is increased. Thus, compared to AT2019dsg, AT2019ehz more clearly separates two physical routes to detectability: a photon-rich route that enhances neutrino production, and a transparent route that favors escaping GeV-to-TeV photons. Within the ASASSN–14li parameter sequence explored here, the source occupies a different regime. In the explored parameter space, the neutrino-bright models do not naturally become CTAO-bright. The most promising electromagnetic counterpart is instead in the MeV-to-GeV band, where primary inverse-Compton emission, pion-induced cascades, and secondary-pair synchrotron can all contribute. This makes ASASSN–14li a useful reminder that neutrino-bright TDEs need not be TeV-bright TDEs. The radio data provide an additional constraint, but they do not uniquely select a leptonic or hadronic solution. Primary-electron synchrotron is sufficient to account for the radio points at the level needed in our exploratory modelling, yet previous studies have interpreted the radio emission of ASASSN–14li in terms of either an outflow or compact jet-like activity ( Alexander et al., 2016 ; van Velzen et al., 2016 ; Krolik et al., 2016 ; Pasham and van Velzen, 2018 ) . In our models, magnetically enhanced configurations can also allow proton synchrotron or secondary pairs to contribute at low frequencies. Rather than a dedicated relativistic jet calculation, we use ASASSN–14li to test whether a compact non-thermal shock can explain the radio-to-high-energy SED within X-ray and γ \gamma -ray constraints. Primary electron synchrotron emission in our reference model broadly matches the radio data, though this represents a consistency check rather than a unique physical origin. Future radio light curves and spectra are therefore essential for separating the location and physical origin of the radio-emitting plasma.

sections.heading: 5.3 γ \gamma -ray  and neutrino detections
sections.text: The possible association of AT2019dsg with IceCube-191001A motivated many of these theoretical developments ( Stein and others, 2021 ) . Additional proposed associations, such as AT2019fdr and AT2019aalc, strengthened the motivation for considering accretion flares as neutrino sources ( Reusch and others, 2022 ; van Velzen and others, 2024 ) . At the same time, the statistical status of these associations remains uncertain ( Abbasi and others, 2025 ) . Updated neutrino reconstructions and catalogues can change the spatial consistency of individual events, and recent IceCube updates motivate treating the proposed associations as suggestive rather than established ( Abbasi and others, 2025 ) . Our results are therefore best interpreted as a detectability study rather than as a claim that any of the modelled sources must have produced a specific IceCube event. The absence of robust GeV detections from optically selected TDEs is another important point. Searches with Fermi /LAT have found no significant GeV emission from samples of candidate neutrino-associated TDEs and from broader TDE samples, leading to upper limits that strongly constrain transparent hadronic scenarios ( Peng et al., 2022 ) . Time-dependent cascade calculations have also shown that Fermi /LAT limits can constrain the emission radius and the maximum energy of the accelerated protons, and that the corresponding expected neutrino event numbers can be small for many configurations ( Yuan and Winter, 2023 ) . Our models follow the same physical logic: the neutrino-bright cases are allowed only if the high-energy photons are either emitted during a short observing window, shifted into the MeV band, or absorbed and reprocessed inside the source. The ASASSN–14li models illustrate this particularly well, because they can be relevant for KM3NeT and Fermi/LAT while remaining below the CTAO benchmark. This motivates a special role for the MeV band. Several TDE neutrino models predict that hidden or partially hidden hadronic activity should be accompanied by hard X-ray or soft γ \gamma -ray emission rather than by an easily detectable TeV counterpart ( Murase et al., 2020 ; Yuan and Winter, 2023 ) . COSI will operate in the soft γ \gamma -ray range and is designed to explore the MeV sky with improved sensitivity, spectroscopy, and sky coverage ( Tomsick and others, 2023 ) . In the context of our models, a COSI detection would be especially valuable because it would probe the cascade and primary inverse-Compton components that sit between the thermal X-ray/UV emission and the GeV-to-TeV band. Conversely, a COSI non-detection during a nearby TDE would help rule out the more luminous hidden-cascade configurations, even if Fermi /LAT and CTAO do not detect the source. Finally, CTAO and KM3NeT provide complementary tests. CTAO will improve transient very-high-energy γ \gamma -ray sensitivity and will be important for rapid follow-up of multi-messenger alerts ( Carosi et al., 2021 ) . KM3NeT/ARCA will provide strong sensitivity to TeV-to-PeV neutrinos from the southern sky ( Aiello and others, 2024 ) . The models presented here show that the best candidates for joint CTAO–KM3NeT detection are not necessarily the most luminous optical TDEs, but the ones in which a hard proton population coexists with a moderately transparent emission region. In contrast, sources with high internal opacity may be better targets for COSI and Fermi /LAT, even when their neutrino flux is high.

sections.heading: 6 Summary and conclusions
sections.text: We have explored the conditions under which TDEs can reveal their hidden non-thermal engines through MeV, GeV, and TeV γ \gamma -ray emission and high-energy neutrinos. Our goal was not to obtain a unique best-fitting model for each event, but to identify the physical regimes in which TDEs become promising targets for COSI, Fermi /LAT, CTAO, and KM3NeT. To this end, we applied a lepto-hadronic emission framework to three representative sources: AT2019dsg, a neutrino-motivated TDE; AT2019ehz, a prompt optical/UV outburst with high-energy detectability potential; and ASASSN–14li, a radio–X-ray bright event with strong constraints on the low-frequency synchrotron component. The main conclusions of this work are as follows. 1. TDEs become high-energy sources only in restricted regions of parameter space. The key parameters are the proton spectral index, the minimum Lorentz factor of the non-thermal protons, the fraction of dissipated power injected into non-thermal particles, the acceleration efficiency, the compactness of the target photon field, and the magnetic field strength. Hard proton spectra and/or large values of γ p , min \gamma_{p,\rm min} move more proton power above the pion-production threshold and therefore favour both multi-TeV neutrino production and hadronic γ \gamma -ray emission. 2. Neutrino-bright does not necessarily mean TeV-bright. Dense optical/UV/X-ray photon fields increase the efficiency of p ​ γ p\gamma interactions and can enhance the neutrino luminosity. However, the same fields also increase the internal γ ​ γ \gamma\gamma opacity and can reprocess the associated γ \gamma -ray emission into lower-energy cascade radiation. The observational outcome therefore depends on the competition between proton cooling, particle escape, and photon attenuation. A TeV non-detection should not be interpreted automatically as evidence for a neutrino-quiet TDE. 3. AT2019dsg provides the benchmark for a neutrino-motivated TDE. In the explored models, several different parameter combinations produce ν μ + ν ¯ μ \nu_{\mu}+\bar{\nu}_{\mu} spectra close to or above the KM3NeT/ARCA reference curve. Models with hard protons, enhanced γ p , min \gamma_{p,\rm min} , or efficient acceleration can also reach the Fermi /LAT and CTAO benchmark sensitivities. The leptonic comparison model remains GeV-bright but neutrino-quiet, showing that a GeV counterpart alone would not uniquely imply efficient hadronic acceleration. 4. AT2019ehz is the clearest TeV-orientated source in our sample. The hadronic models of AT2019ehz can become CTAO- and KM3NeT-relevant when the proton spectrum is hard or when the low-energy part of the proton distribution is suppressed. The comparison between cold-corona and no-corona cases highlights the central tension of TDE multimessenger emission: photon-rich environments favour neutrino production, while more transparent environments favour escaping GeV-to-TeV photons. 5. ASASSN–14li probes a different regime. In contrast to AT2019dsg and AT2019ehz, ASASSN–14li is most naturally bright in the MeV-to-GeV band among the compact shock models explored here. Its reference Model A is relevant for COSI, Fermi /LAT, and KM3NeT, while the source remains at most marginal for CTAO. The radio data are broadly consistent with primary-electron synchrotron emission, but they do not uniquely determine the emission channel. In magnetically enhanced models, proton synchrotron and synchrotron emission from secondary pairs can also contribute at radio-to-infrared frequencies. 6. The MeV band is a key diagnostic of hidden hadronic activity. If TeV photons are absorbed inside the source, a fraction of the hadronic power can emerge through electromagnetic cascades at hard-X-ray and MeV energies. COSI will therefore probe a regime that is complementary to Fermi /LAT and CTAO. In this sense, the absence of a TeV signal and the presence of an MeV excess would be a powerful clue that the source is partially hidden rather than intrinsically weak. 7. Benchmark proximity is not a detection claim. We quantified the models using the maximum ratio between the predicted flux and the reference sensitivity curve in each band. This provides a compact way to compare models, but it does not replace a time-dependent detectability calculation. For transient sources, the relevant quantities are the active duration, observing cadence, background level, source position, and, for neutrinos, the flavour-dependent effective area and expected event number. Overall, our results suggest that TDEs can appear in several distinct multimessenger regimes. Some are transparent enough to shine in GeV–TeV γ \gamma rays and neutrinos; some are hidden enough to produce neutrinos and MeV cascades without a strong TeV counterpart; and some are predominantly leptonic, producing GeV emission with little associated neutrino flux. The same source class can therefore look very different to COSI, Fermi /LAT, CTAO, KM3NeT, and radio telescopes, depending on where and when the non-thermal particles are accelerated. Further studies will be essential for determining whether TDEs are rare, spectacular multimessenger engines, a subdominant contribution to the diffuse neutrino sky, or both. Acknowledgements. sections.heading: Appendix A Detailed radiative-component decompositions
sections.text: This appendix shows the full component decompositions of the reference Model A used for each source. These figures are not separate fits; they expose the individual radiative channels that are grouped or omitted in the simplified SED panels shown in the main text. In all panels, the thick black curve shows the total model spectrum. The primary electron synchrotron and inverse-Compton components are shown by green and blue dashed curves, respectively. The p ​ p pp channel is represented by the red dashed π 0 \pi^{0} -decay component and by the red dotted synchrotron emission from secondary pairs. The p ​ γ p\gamma channel is represented by the purple dashed π 0 \pi^{0} -decay component and by the purple dotted synchrotron emission from secondary pairs. When visible, proton synchrotron radiation is shown by a magenta dash-dotted curve. The thermal disc, black-body, and coronal photon fields are shown by grey dashed, red dash-dotted, and grey dotted curves, respectively.

sections.heading: A.1 AT2019dsg
sections.text: Figure 14 shows the full decomposition of the reference AT2019dsg Model A. The high-energy emission is dominated by the photohadronic p ​ γ → π 0 p\gamma\rightarrow\pi^{0} component in the CTAO band, while the p ​ p pp channel and secondary-pair synchrotron emission remain subdominant. The decomposition therefore clarifies the connection between the TeV γ \gamma -ray component and the multi-TeV neutrino spectrum discussed in the main text. Figure 14: Full radiative-component decomposition of the reference AT2019dsg Model A. The line styles identify the primary leptonic emission, p ​ p pp components, p ​ γ p\gamma components, proton synchrotron radiation, and the thermal/coronal photon fields.

sections.heading: A.2 AT2019ehz
sections.text: Figure 15 shows the full decomposition of the reference AT2019ehz Model A. The cold corona supplies an additional target photon field for photohadronic interactions and also contributes to the internal opacity. The CTAO-band emission is mainly associated with p ​ γ → π 0 p\gamma\rightarrow\pi^{0} decay, while the secondary-pair components trace the electromagnetic cascade initiated by hadronic interactions and photon–photon absorption. Figure 15: Full radiative-component decomposition of the reference AT2019ehz Model A. The line styles identify the primary leptonic emission, p ​ p pp components, p ​ γ p\gamma components, proton synchrotron radiation, and the thermal/coronal photon fields.

sections.heading: A.3 ASASSN–14li
sections.text: Figure 16 shows the full decomposition of the reference ASASSN–14li Model A. This source differs from AT2019dsg and AT2019ehz because the neutrino-bright configurations remain comparatively faint in the CTAO band. The decomposition is useful for separating the primary inverse-Compton component, which shapes the MeV–GeV emission, from the hadronic components that contribute to the high-energy tail and to the neutrino output. It also illustrates how internal photon–photon absorption and subsequent cascading can redistribute power away from the TeV band. Figure 16: Full radiative-component decomposition of the reference ASASSN–14li Model A. The line styles identify the primary leptonic emission, p ​ p pp components, p ​ γ p\gamma components, secondary-pair synchrotron radiation, and the thermal photon fields.

sections.heading: B.1.1 High-energy spectral energy distributions
sections.text: Figure 17 shows the SEDs of the four AT2019dsg models (B–E). In each panel, the thick black line is the total model spectrum. The thermal emission from the disc is shown by a grey dashed curve, the black-body component by a red dash-dotted curve, and the coronal emission, when present, by a grey dotted curve. The thin grey curves mark the COSI, Fermi/LAT, and CTAO reference sensitivities indicated in the panels. The remaining curves show the high-energy components that dominate each model: neutral-pion decay from p ​ p pp interactions is shown by a red dashed line, neutral-pion decay from p ​ γ p\gamma interactions by a purple dashed line, and synchrotron emission from secondary pairs by dotted curves. In the leptonic Model E, the green dashed and blue dashed curves show the primary electron synchrotron and inverse-Compton components, respectively. Model B demonstrates that, for a softer proton spectrum with p p = 2 p_{\rm p}=2 , a much larger γ p , min \gamma_{p,\rm min} is needed to concentrate the non-thermal proton power near energies relevant for pion production. In this case, both p ​ p pp and p ​ γ p\gamma channels contribute in the CTAO range, but the requirement of a high low-energy cutoff makes the model less natural than Model A. Model C reaches a similar goal by increasing the fraction of power placed into non-thermal protons. This boosts the secondary synchrotron and pion-decay components while keeping γ p , min \gamma_{p,\rm min} lower than in Model B. Model D shows that even a low γ p , min \gamma_{p,\rm min} can yield an observable high-energy component if the acceleration is more efficient and the proton distribution extends to the photohadronic regime. Finally, Model E illustrates a different detectability regime: the GeV emission is produced mainly by the primary electron inverse-Compton component, while the hadronic and neutrino outputs are negligible. This model is therefore relevant for Fermi/LAT searches but is not expected to be a promising KM3NeT source. Figure 17: Spectral energy distributions of the four exploratory Models B–E for AT2019dsg. The thick black line shows the total model emission after accounting for absorption. The thermal disc, black-body, and coronal components are shown by dashed grey, dash-dotted red, and dotted grey curves, respectively. Hadronic γ \gamma -ray components are shown by red and purple curves: dashed red for p ​ p → π 0 pp\rightarrow\pi^{0} , purple dashed for p ​ γ → π 0 p\gamma\rightarrow\pi^{0} , and dotted curves for synchrotron radiation from secondary pairs. In Model E the green and blue dashed curves show the synchrotron and inverse-Compton emission of primary electrons. The thin grey curves indicate the COSI ( Tomsick and others, 2023 ) , Fermi/LAT, and CTAO reference sensitivities.

sections.heading: B.1.2 Muon-neutrino predictions
B.1.3 Particle distributions and maximum energies in the reference model
sections.text: To illustrate how the high-energy emission is produced, Fig. 19 shows the particle distributions and acceleration/cooling timescales for Model A. The electron distribution is dominated by primary electrons at low kinetic energies. Secondary pairs produced in p ​ p pp interactions populate the GeV-to-TeV kinetic-energy range, while the p ​ γ p\gamma channel contributes at higher energies once the proton distribution crosses the photomeson threshold. The γ ​ γ \gamma\gamma pairs form at lower electron energies and trace the internal absorption of high-energy photons. The proton distribution is broad and hard, as expected for p p = 1.7 p_{\rm p}=1.7 , and cuts off in the PeV range. The timescale panels show why this model can generate both TeV gamma rays and neutrinos. For electrons, the maximum energy is determined by the balance between acceleration and synchrotron cooling; escape is slower and therefore does not set the electron cutoff. For protons, synchrotron and p ​ p pp cooling are inefficient over most of the relevant energy range. The maximum energy is instead controlled mainly by the competition between acceleration and escape, with p ​ γ p\gamma losses becoming important only close to the highest energies. Thus the model is not a full proton calorimeter, but it accelerates protons efficiently enough to enter the photohadronic regime before they escape. This explains why the same configuration can produce a CTAO-relevant γ \gamma -ray component and a neutrino spectrum close to the KM3NeT/ARCA benchmark. (a) Electron distribution. (b) Proton distribution. (c) Electron timescales. (d) Proton timescales. Figure 19: Particle distributions and acceleration/cooling timescales for the reference AT2019dsg Model A. The top panels show E i 2 ​ d ​ n i / d ​ E i E_{i}^{2}\,dn_{i}/dE_{i} for electrons and protons. Primary electrons are shown in blue, secondary pairs from p ​ p pp interactions in orange, secondary pairs from p ​ γ p\gamma interactions in red, and pairs from γ ​ γ \gamma\gamma absorption in purple. The bottom panels show the acceleration, escape, synchrotron, p ​ p pp , and p ​ γ p\gamma timescales, as labelled in the panels. The vertical grey dotted line marks the adopted maximum energy. The five models therefore map out three qualitatively different regimes. First, hard proton spectra with moderate γ p , min \gamma_{p,\rm min} can place both the γ \gamma -ray and neutrino components near the sensitivity of CTAO and KM3NeT, as in Model A. Second, soft proton spectra can reach comparable fluxes, but only by increasing either the γ p , min \gamma_{p,\rm min} or the fraction of non-thermal power injected into protons, as in Models B and C. Third, GeV γ \gamma -ray detectability does not imply neutrino detectability: Model E can approach the Fermi/LAT band through primary electron inverse-Compton emission while remaining neutrino quiet. This separation between GeV-bright and neutrino-bright configurations will be useful when comparing AT2019dsg to AT2019ehz below.

sections.heading: B.2.1 High-energy spectral energy distributions of AT2019ehz
sections.text: The SEDs of the four AT2019ehz models (B–E) are shown in Fig. 20 . The line styles follow those used for AT2019dsg. The thick black curve shows the total model spectrum, the grey dashed curve shows the thermal disc, the red dash-dotted curve shows the additional black-body component, and the grey dotted curve shows the corona when present. The hadronic components are shown by red and purple curves: red dashed for p ​ p → π 0 pp\rightarrow\pi^{0} , purple dashed for p ​ γ → π 0 p\gamma\rightarrow\pi^{0} , and dotted curves for synchrotron radiation from secondary pairs. In panels where primary leptonic components are shown, the green dashed and blue dashed curves represent primary electron synchrotron and inverse-Compton emission. The thin grey curves indicate the COSI, Fermi/LAT, and CTAO reference sensitivities. Model B shows the effect of removing the corona while keeping a hard proton spectrum. The reduced coronal opacity allows a larger fraction of the high-energy photons to escape, and the combination of η = 4 \eta=4 and f sc = 10 − 3 f_{\rm sc}=10^{-3} makes the model relevant across the Fermi/LAT and CTAO bands. This model is therefore the most direct multimessenger showcase in the AT2019ehz set, but we do not use it as the reference case because it relies on a more transparent environment. Model C demonstrates that a soft proton spectrum can still produce CTAO-relevant emission if the low-energy part of the proton distribution is suppressed by increasing γ p , min \gamma_{p,\rm min} to 500. Model D reaches the high-energy band through a different route: it keeps a soft proton spectrum but increases the non-thermal proton fraction to ε p = 0.8 \varepsilon_{p}=0.8 , boosting both the secondary-pair synchrotron and pion-decay components. Model E is qualitatively different. Its high-energy emission is concentrated mainly in the Fermi/LAT range and the infrared band receives a visible contribution from synchrotron radiation of secondary pairs produced in p ​ p pp interactions. This case therefore illustrates that a GeV-detectable TDE does not necessarily have to be a strong TeV or neutrino source. Figure 20: Spectral energy distributions of the four exploratory Models B–E for AT2019ehz. The thick black line shows the total model emission. The thermal disc, black-body, and coronal components are shown by grey dashed, red dash-dotted, and grey dotted curves, respectively. Hadronic γ \gamma -ray components are shown by red and purple curves: red dashed for p ​ p → π 0 pp\rightarrow\pi^{0} , purple dashed for p ​ γ → π 0 p\gamma\rightarrow\pi^{0} , and dotted curves for synchrotron radiation from secondary pairs. The thin grey curves indicate the COSI ( Tomsick and others, 2023 ) , Fermi/LAT, and CTAO reference sensitivities.

sections.heading: B.2.2 Muon-neutrino predictions
B.3.1 High-energy spectral energy distributions
sections.text: The SEDs of the three (B–D) ASASSN–14li models are shown in Fig. 22 . The line styles follow those used for AT2019dsg and AT2019ehz. The thick black curve shows the total model spectrum. The grey dashed and red dash-dotted curves show the thermal disc and black-body components, respectively. Primary electron synchrotron and inverse-Compton emission are shown by green and blue dashed curves when visible. Hadronic components are shown in red and purple: red dashed curves show p ​ p → π 0 pp\rightarrow\pi^{0} , purple dashed curves show p ​ γ → π 0 p\gamma\rightarrow\pi^{0} , and red dotted curves show synchrotron emission from secondary pairs produced in p ​ p pp interactions. The thin grey curves indicate the COSI, Fermi/LAT, and CTAO reference sensitivities. Model B tests whether a large non-thermal proton fraction can compensate for a substantially lower jet power. The high-energy SED is again hadronically dominated, but the total flux remains below the CTAO reference curve. Model C explores a different extreme: the jet power and γ p , min \gamma_{p,\rm min} are increased, and the plasma beta is reduced to β = 0.1 \beta=0.1 , corresponding to a more magnetically dominated emitting region. This boosts the hadronic contribution and produces a broad GeV-to-TeV component, but even this configuration does not give a robust CTAO detection in our setup. Finally, Model D is qualitatively different. Its high-energy output is dominated by primary electron inverse-Compton emission, while the hadronic normalization is weak. This model can therefore be relevant for Fermi/LAT searches, but it is not expected to be a neutrino-bright source. Figure 22: Spectral energy distributions of the three exploratory Models B–D for ASASSN–14li. The thick black line shows the total model emission. The thermal disc and black-body components are shown by grey dashed and red dash-dotted curves, respectively. Primary electron synchrotron and inverse-Compton emission are shown by green and blue dashed curves when visible. Hadronic γ \gamma -ray components are shown by red and purple curves: red dashed for p ​ p → π 0 pp\rightarrow\pi^{0} , purple dashed for p ​ γ → π 0 p\gamma\rightarrow\pi^{0} , and red dotted for synchrotron radiation from secondary pairs produced in p ​ p pp interactions. The radio data are broadly consistent with primary electron synchrotron, although additional synchrotron components, such as proton synchrotron in Model C, may also contribute. The thin grey curves indicate the COSI ( Tomsick and others, 2023 ) , Fermi/LAT, and CTAO reference sensitivities.

Motivated by recent candidate TDE–neutrino associations and by the forthcoming sensitivity of multimessenger facilities, we investigate under which physical conditions TDEs can be detected in MeV, GeV, and TeV gamma rays, and in high-energy neutrinos. We develop a lepto-hadronic emission framework and apply it to three representative sources: AT2019dsg, AT2019ehz, and ASASSN-14li. For each source we explore a set of physically motivated models that vary the proton and electron spectral indices, the minimum Lorentz factor of non-thermal protons, the particle energy partition, the acceleration efficiency, the magnetic compactness, and the presence of a compact corona. We compute the broadband spectral energy distributions, the associated muon-neutrino spectra, and compare them with reference sensitivities for COSI, Fermi/LAT, CTAO, and KM3NeT/ARCA. We find that hard proton spectra and/or large minimum proton Lorentz factors are the most favourable conditions for TeV gamma-ray and neutrino detectability, while GeV-bright models can be predominantly leptonic and neutrino quiet. AT2019dsg and AT2019ehz can reach the CTAO and KM3NeT benchmarks in hadronically favourable configurations, whereas ASASSN-14li is more naturally bright in the MeV–GeV band and constrained by its radio synchrotron emission. Our results highlight the importance of combining MeV, GeV, TeV, radio, and neutrino observations to distinguish between transparent, hidden, and lepton-dominated TDE emission regimes. Key Words. Acceleration of particles – accretion – black hole physics – neutrinos 1 Introduction Tidal disruption events (TDEs) occur when a star is scattered close enough to a massive black hole that the tidal force exceeds the star’s self-gravity. A fraction of the stellar debris remains bound, returns to pericenter, circularizes, and can power a luminous flare from the otherwise faint nucleus of a galaxy ( Rees, 1988 ) . Because the debris initially falls back at highly super-Eddington rates for many systems, TDEs provide a transient view of accretion, outflows, shocks, and non-thermal particle acceleration around massive black holes. Wide-field optical surveys and rapid multiwavelength follow-up have shown that TDEs are not a single observational class: some events are dominated by optical/UV emission, some are X-ray bright, some launch radio-emitting outflows or jets, and only a few have been discussed as possible high-energy neutrino emitters ( Langis and others, 2026 ) . The origin of the optical/UV emission remains one of the central open questions in TDE physics. In the simplest picture, the observed luminosity would trace efficient accretion of the fallback material, but the radiated energy and characteristic temperatures of optical TDEs are often difficult to reconcile with a bare, compact, steady thin disc ( Mummery et al., 2025 ) . Several alternatives have therefore been proposed. The optical/UV flare may be powered, at least partly, by shocks produced during stream self-intersection and circularization ( Shiokawa et al., 2015 ; Piran et al., 2015 ) ; by reprocessing of inner-disc or coronal radiation in an extended photosphere, wind, or debris layer; or by a combination of accretion, shocks, and outflow emission whose relative importance changes with time and viewing angle. Magnetic fields can further modify this picture by affecting the returning debris stream and the subsequent circularization flow ( Guillochon and McCourt, 2017 ; Bonnerot et al., 2017 ) . Recent optical polarimetric observations have strengthened the case that at least some TDEs require non-axisymmetric geometries and shock-powered emission during disc formation ( Liodakis and others, 2023 ; Koljonen and others, 2024 ; Koljonen et al., 2025 ; Floris and others, 2025 ; Floris and others, 2026 ) . These uncertainties are important for high-energy modelling because they determine the photon fields, magnetic fields, and compactness that control both particle cooling and γ \gamma -ray absorption. TDEs have also been proposed as sources of cosmic rays and high-energy neutrinos. Early studies focused on relativistic TDE jets and considered whether protons accelerated in internal shocks or external outflows could produce neutrinos through p γ \gamma and pp interactions ( Farrar and Gruzinov, 2009 ; Wang et al., 2011 ; Farrar and Piran, 2014 ; Wang and Liu, 2016 ; Dai and Fang, 2017 ; Senno et al., 2017 ; Lunardini and Winter, 2017 ; Guépin et al., 2018 ; Biehl et al., 2018 ) . Subsequent work showed that the same basic idea can be realised in several physical environments, including choked or off-axis jets, coronae, radiatively inefficient accretion flows, disc winds, and debris-interaction regions ( Hayasaki and Yamazaki, 2019 ; Murase et al., 2020 ; Liu et al., 2020 ; Fang et al., 2020 ; Winter and Lunardini, 2021 ; Matsumoto et al., 2022 ; Winter and Lunardini, 2023 ; Zheng et al., 2023 ; Mukhopadhyay et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Yuan et al., 2024 ) . These models differ in geometry, target photon field, baryon loading, and internal opacity, but they share a common observational challenge: neutrino production is accompanied by electromagnetic cascades, and the escaping γ \gamma -ray emission must remain consistent with X-ray, MeV, GeV, and TeV constraints. The possible association of AT2019dsg with IceCube-191001A brought this question into sharper focus ( Stein and others, 2021 ) . Further candidate associations involving accretion flares or TDE-like nuclear transients, such as AT2019fdr and AT2019aalc, have strengthened the motivation for considering TDEs as neutrino sources ( Reusch and others, 2022 ; van Velzen and others, 2024 ) . At the same time, the statistical significance of individual associations remains debated. Updated IceCube event catalogues, Fermi /LAT non-detections, and population-level correlation studies all indicate that current TDE–neutrino associations should be treated as suggestive rather than established ( Peng et al., 2022 ; Abbasi and others, 2025 ; Lu et al., 2025 ; Langis et al., 2026 ; Mukhopadhyay et al., 2026 ) . This motivates a question that is broader than the interpretation of any single event: under which physical conditions should a TDE be detectable in γ \gamma rays and neutrinos at all? A particularly useful diagnostic is the energy band in which the non-thermal power escapes. If the source is transparent, pion-decay emission and inverse-Compton radiation can appear in the GeV–TeV range and may be constrained by Fermi /LAT or detected by CTAO. If the source is compact and photon rich, the same hadronic activity can be hidden at TeV energies and reprocessed into the hard X-ray or MeV band through pair production and electromagnetic cascades ( Murase et al., 2020 ; Yuan and Winter, 2023 ) . The MeV range is therefore a key bridge between thermal X-ray/UV emission and GeV–TeV searches. Future observations with the Compton Spectrometer and Imager (COSI) will be especially valuable for testing hidden or partially hidden TDE scenarios ( Tomsick and others, 2023 ) , while CTAO and KM3NeT/ARCA will probe complementary TeV γ \gamma -ray and TeV–PeV neutrino signatures ( Carosi et al., 2021 ; Aiello and others, 2024 ) . In this paper we explore the detectability of non-thermal emission from TDEs using a lepto-hadronic emission framework based on the steady-state multi-zone bhjet model and its hadronic extension ( Lucchini et al., 2022 ; Kantzas and others, 2020 ; Kantzas et al., 2023b ) . Our aim is not to obtain a unique fit to each source, nor to claim that any individual TDE must have produced a particular neutrino alert. Instead, each model is a representative or reference realization chosen to isolate a specific physical regime, such as MeV–GeV brightness, TeV transparency, neutrino production, or radio synchrotron consistency. We use these representative models to identify the combinations of particle acceleration, proton spectral shape, minimum proton Lorentz factor, energy partition, magnetic field, photon compactness, and coronal opacity that make a TDE visible to COSI, Fermi /LAT, CTAO, and KM3NeT. This parameter-space approach is designed to connect the intrinsic physics of the source to practical multimessenger detectability. The overplotted multiwavelength data are used to check whether the model normalization and spectral shape are broadly compatible with the observed emission during the selected epoch, but the models are not selected by minimizing a global likelihood or chi-square. We apply the model to three TDEs that represent different observational regimes. AT2019dsg is used as a neutrino-motivated benchmark because of its proposed association with IceCube-191001A and evidence for non-thermal activity. AT2019ehz is treated as a prompt optical/UV outburst case with X-ray follow-up, allowing us to test whether high-energy emission could accompany the main TDE flare even without an established neutrino association. Finally, ASASSN–14li provides an X-ray- and radio-bright benchmark. Its radio data constrain the low-energy synchrotron component and allow us to test whether primary electrons, secondary pairs, or proton synchrotron can contribute to the observed non-thermal emission. In Sect. 3 , we summarize the multiwavelength data used for the three sources. In Sect. 4 , we present the model families, spectral energy distributions, neutrino predictions, and benchmark-proximity ratios for COSI, Fermi /LAT, CTAO, and KM3NeT. We discuss the physical interpretation and comparison with previous work in Sect. 5 , and we summarize our conclusions in Sect. 6 . 2 Model We use a semi-analytical, steady-state lepto-hadronic model to calculate the intrinsic photon and neutrino emission from compact dissipation regions in TDE environments. The model follows the philosophy of bhjet , where the dynamical properties of the emitting plasma are coupled to radiative transfer, but it is adapted here to the geometry expected during the circularization and early accretion phase of a TDE rather than to a scale-invariant compact jet ( Lucchini et al., 2022 ) . The hadronic extension follows the treatment developed in Kantzas and others (2020) , where relativistic protons are accelerated together with electrons and interact with gas and radiation fields, producing secondary photons, pairs, and neutrinos. The goal of the present work is not to fit a unique solution for each source, but to identify the physical conditions under which the GeV-to-TeV γ \gamma -ray and neutrino emission can become observable. 2.1 Geometry and dynamical assumptions We consider a TDE around a black hole of mass M BH M_{\rm BH} and define the gravitational radius as R g = G ​ M BH / c 2 R_{g}=GM_{\rm BH}/c^{2} . During the circularization of the stellar debris, shocks are expected to form in the accretion flow and/or in the stream-intersection region ( Shiokawa et al., 2015 ; Steinberg and Stone, 2024 ) . We describe the system with an accretion disk in the equatorial plane and use the angle θ \theta between the disk axis and the line of sight as the viewing angle. Thus, θ ≃ 0 ∘ \theta\simeq 0^{\circ} corresponds to a face-on system, whereas θ ≃ 90 ∘ \theta\simeq 90^{\circ} corresponds to an edge-on system. The disk is truncated at a characteristic radius R disk R_{\rm disk} and radiates with luminosity L disk L_{\rm disk} , with the thermal component peaking in the optical/UV band for the parameter range explored here. In addition to the disk radiation, we include a compact thermal corona. The corona is described by its radius R cor R_{\rm cor} , temperature T cor T_{\rm cor} , and Thomson optical depth τ cor \tau_{\rm cor} . The corresponding number density is n cor = τ cor / σ T ​ R cor n_{\rm cor}=\tau_{\rm cor}/\sigma_{T}R_{\rm cor} , where σ T \sigma_{T} is the Thomson cross section. Unless stated otherwise, we assume a charge-neutral plasma with equal numbers of thermal electrons and protons. The thermal electrons Comptonize the disk photons and provide an additional target field for inverse Compton scattering and photohadronic interactions. In the numerical examples below the coronal temperature should be interpreted as an electron thermal energy, k B ​ T cor k_{\rm B}T_{\rm cor} , and is therefore quoted in energy units. The dissipation region and the corona should not be interpreted as two independent acceleration zones. In the present implementation, non-thermal electrons and protons are accelerated only in the compact shock region located at radius R R . The corona, when included, acts as a thermal photon field and as a reservoir of thermal target protons for Compton scattering, photohadronic interactions, and pp interactions. Its characteristic radius is denoted by R cor R_{\rm cor} . Thus, models with R < R cor R<R_{\rm cor} correspond to dissipation embedded within the coronal environment, whereas models with R > R cor R>R_{\rm cor} place the shock outside the nominal coronal scale. This distinction affects the target photon density, the internal opacity, and the efficiency of hadronic interactions, but protons are not separately accelerated throughout the corona. We assume that a fraction of the power released during the TDE is dissipated in shocks located at a characteristic radius R R from the black hole. This radius also sets the escape length of particles from the acceleration region. The dissipated power available to non-thermal particles and magnetic fields is denoted by P TDE P_{\mathrm{TDE}} . We parametrize the partition between particle and magnetic pressure through the plasma beta, β = P particles / P magnetic \beta=P_{\rm particles}/P_{\rm magnetic} . Low values of β \beta correspond to magnetically dominated shocks, while high values of β \beta correspond to particle-dominated shocks. We further use the parameter η e \eta_{e} to control the relative amount of non-thermal power carried by electrons and protons. This parameter is important for the high-energy output because the GeV emission can be dominated by leptonic inverse Compton scattering, whereas the TeV and neutrino emission require an efficient hadronic component. The emitting region is treated as quasi-static in the source frame. Therefore, the calculations presented here do not include quantities associated with a relativistic jet. The framework is intended to describe compact disk/corona, circularization, or mildly outflowing shock regions rather than a fully relativistic jetted TDE. 2.2 Particle acceleration At the shocks, a fraction of the thermal particles is accelerated to non-thermal energies. For the full synchrotron emissivity we use the analytical expressions of Blumenthal and Gould (1970) for both electrons and protons, although the proton synchrotron component is generally subdominant for the parameters considered here ( Muecke et al., 2003 ) . The same non-thermal electrons inverse-Compton scatter the synchrotron photons, disk photons, and coronal photons. We include the transition from the Thomson to the Klein–Nishina regime in the calculation of the emitted spectrum and in the cooling time-scale. This leptonic channel is particularly important in the GeV band, especially when the magnetic field is weak enough for inverse Compton cooling to compete with synchrotron cooling. Relativistic protons interact with both gas and radiation. Inelastic proton-proton collisions occur on the thermal protons of the corona, disk atmosphere, or debris environment, while photohadronic interactions occur on the synchrotron, disk, and coronal photon fields. These interactions produce charged and neutral pions. Neutral pions decay into γ \gamma rays, while charged pions decay into neutrinos and secondary pairs. We use the semi-analytical prescription of Kelner et al. (2006) , with the updated cross sections of Kafexhiu et al. (2014) , for pp interactions and the prescription of Kelner and Aharonian (2008) for p γ \gamma interactions. The resulting secondary electrons and positrons are followed radiatively, allowing electromagnetic cascades to redistribute part of the hadronic power to lower photon energies. The neutrino spectrum is calculated consistently with the charged-pion component of the pp and p γ \gamma interactions. At production, the flavor composition is dominated by the pion-decay chain, while at Earth we assume standard flavor mixing, leading approximately to equal fluxes of electron, muon, and tau neutrinos. For a source at luminosity distance d L d_{L} , the all-flavor neutrino energy flux is obtained from the intrinsic neutrino luminosity through the usual geometric dilution. The same physical ingredients that enhance neutrino production, namely high gas density and high photon density, can therefore suppress the escaping γ \gamma -ray flux. This tension is central to the detectability problem addressed in this work: TDEs are most efficient neutrino sources when the hadronic interaction depth is high, but they are most promising TeV γ \gamma -ray sources when the pair-production and matter opacities are low enough for high-energy photons to escape.
